analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors own hospitals they can send their own Medicare patients to.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 42 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote in either committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act bars doctors who own part of a hospital from sending their Medicare patients there, with narrow exceptions. This bill would wipe out those limits, letting physicians build new hospitals they own and refer their own patients to for Medicare-paid care. It sat in two House committees and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who want to invest in hospitals. Lifting the ban would let them own a facility and profit when their own referrals generate Medicare-paid revenue there — imaging, surgery, admissions — which is the profit engine of physician-owned hospitals.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA provisions (Sections 6001 and 10601 and a related reconciliation provision) that restrict Medicare participation by new or expanded physician-owned hospitals, restoring the rules that existed before health care reform as if they had never been passed.

For physician-owners, the whole-hospital exception restored by the bill means their own referrals to their own hospital become Medicare-billable again, turning an ownership stake into referral revenue.
Supporters frame it as expanding patient choice and access to physician-owned facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare (taxpayers and beneficiaries) would bear the cost of higher utilization, since doctors with ownership stakes have a documented financial incentive to order more care — more scans, more procedures, more admissions — at facilities they own. Community hospitals would also lose patients and revenue to competing physician-owned facilities.

drawbacks.text: Physicians with an ownership interest have a financial stake in the volume of care they order; research on self-referral has consistently found that physician-owned facilities generate more imaging, procedures, and spending per episode than non-owned facilities, which is why the limits were enacted in the first place.

The bill does not rewrite the rules; it repeals the reform sections wholesale and restores pre-2010 law as if the limits had never existed, wiping out the entire regulatory structure, including the terms under which existing physician-owned hospitals were allowed to keep operating and the ownership-disclosure requirements.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's benefit accrues to a specific group of investors — physicians who want to own hospitals — while the cost lands diffusely on Medicare spending, and that the bill's title about 'patient access' describes the mechanism (more facilities) while the evidence base on self-referral points the other way on cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated and concrete: physicians gain the right to profit from their own referrals. The costs are diffuse: higher Medicare utilization and spending, and financial pressure on community hospitals that cannot steer their owners' patients. The mechanism this bill restores — doctors referring their own patients to facilities they partly own — is precisely the conflict of interest the 2010 law was written to close, and the bill offers no new safeguard to address it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, moved to a Health Subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 3, 2019, and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels that share jurisdiction over Medicare payment and hospital rules.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it sat; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no further action for the remainder of the Congress.

It drew 42 cosponsors, 39 of them Republicans and 3 of 231 House Democrats, but with no committee action it never reached the House floor, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing ban on physician self-referral stays in force, so Medicare and beneficiaries avoid the higher utilization the bill would have enabled, and community hospitals keep the level playing field the 2010 law created. The physician-investors who backed the bill gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare and community hospitals, whose interests the law protects

for.name: Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 3, 2019, to repeal the ACA's limits on physician-owned hospital self-referral; a physician who has long championed physician-owned hospitals.

for.name: 39 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making Republicans 39 of its 42 cosponsors.

for.name: 3 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a small minority of the Democratic caucus.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Medicare and hospital jurisdiction)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (Medicare payment jurisdiction)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action on the bill.

against.name: Community hospital industry (e.g., the American Hospital Association)
against.what_they_did: The hospital industry has long opposed loosening the self-referral ban, arguing physician-owned hospitals skim profitable, well-insured patients and raise overall health spending.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 39 of 42 cosponsors were House Republicans, versus 3 of 231 House Democrats — and with no votes ever held, the bill's fate was decided by committee inaction rather than a recorded party split.

industries.note: The bill is written entirely for this group: it would let doctors own a hospital and bill Medicare for care they refer there themselves. That ownership stake is a financial incentive to order more care, and the higher utilization shows up as Medicare spending.

Physician-owned competitors would be able to recruit physicians as investors and draw referring doctors away, taking patients and revenue from community hospitals. Community hospitals' interest in keeping the ban protects their market, though the ban also serves a genuine cost-control purpose.
Not an industry, but the bill's main cost falls here: self-referral is associated with more scans, procedures, and admissions, which Medicare pays for.
